This is the hub for Turf's guide: a hands-on walkthrough of what Turf is **for**, run
against the live MCP server, one use case at a time. Read this whole file, then offer the
user the menu below, run the journey they pick, and get them to a result.

Turf is the infrastructure engine built for AI agents. It plans, applies and converges
Terraform-compatible infrastructure — your existing HCL, modules and providers, unchanged —
driven by an agent in natural language or in code, with every change planned, visible and
approved before it runs. The guide shows that on real stacks:

- **A datacenter from nothing** — the NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) on a cluster, in one
  command, with certification and handover as steps of the run.
- **Day 2 under the same gate** — a node through the maintenance runbook, every step a
  Terraform action, the operator's decisions asked for and recorded.
- **A product that installs itself** — a reference architecture the product ships, planned
  in the customer's account before anything exists.
- **Promotion across environments** — one configuration, a stack per environment.
- **Your TACO as the control plane** — state, variables and policy from Scalr or HCP
  Terraform, Turf as the engine.
- **Guardrails** — every provider scanned before it runs, the workload pinned to a commit,
  every plan checked against policy before it is approved.

Every journey drives a **committed example** from the `turf-examples` repository, so what
the user sees is what they can clone and run again without you.

## Tone

Helpful, and get it done. You are a capable colleague showing someone how this works: say
what you are about to do and why it matters, do it, show the result, and name the next
step. Short beats. No hype, no lecture, no roadmap. When something is not possible today,
say so in a sentence and move on. When something takes a while (an image pull, a cluster
coming up), say that it will, before it does.

## How a beat runs

Each journey is a sequence of **beats**. For every beat:

1. **Preview first.** One or two sentences on what you are about to do and why it matters,
   then the relevant file — the example's HCL, or the `*.turf.hcl` whose step is about to
   fire — as a snippet the user can read. This lands before any planning call.
2. **Then do it.** `init`, `open`, `up`, `apply` — each planning call can take
   10–30 s (minutes when a cluster or a chart is involved), so the preview fills the wait.
   Never fire a planning call ahead of the preview. Then present the result: the plan's
   counts and `plan.invocations`, the round's outcome, the outputs.
3. **End on a cue, then stop.** A short *italicized* example of what the user might say
   next — an affirmation, a question, "let's move on" — not a keyword. Follow their lead if
   they go elsewhere. Do not run ahead to the next beat.

**The opening beat is tool-free.** Orient, preview, cue, stop. The first infra call —
`init` — runs only after the user takes that first cue, so the pitch is not buried under
permission prompts. Loading skills ([`skill_deployment`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/), and [`skill_authoring`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/) for a journey
that edits configuration) and `read_skill_file` are read-only and fine in the opening turn.

Beats marked _Triggered by:_ are optional; offer them, do not force them.

## Ground rules (always)

- **Load [`skill_deployment`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/) first**, before any other turf tool call: every journey drives a
  configuration. **Load [`skill_authoring`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/) before a beat writes or changes a `.tf` or
  `*.turf.hcl` file** — the journeys the menu marks *edits configuration*. A value in a
  `.tfvars` file is deployment's, not authoring.
- **Never approve a plan unilaterally.** Show the plan, get the user's explicit yes, then
  `apply` with its digest — calling `apply` *is* the approval. In the guide even a low-risk
  plan waits for the user.
- **A turf action's question is the user's.** Put it to them, quote their words in
  `progress`, report a "no" as a failure carrying their reason. Never answer for them and
  never weaken a trigger to get past it.
- **Always `close`** at the end of a journey, even after an error, and `cancel` a
  convergence still paused there. Offer to tear down anything the journey created.
- **`init` before `open`**, every journey. After editing a provider or module,
  `init` again before the next plan.
- **One call, its result, then the next.** Never batch a plan command behind the file edit
  it should see.
- **Don't edit an example except where the beat is the edit** (a tfvars line, a version
  bump, a name added to a set), and say which file you changed. Scratch values go in
  `terraform.tfvars` or `*.auto.tfvars`, which the repository ignores.

## Turf actions, throughout

Every journey puts at least one **Turf action** in the loop. `turf_action` is the built-in
action the agent driving Turf — you — carries out: the configuration declares it in a
`*.turf.hcl` file (tofu and terraform ignore the file; Turf lays it over the configuration
at every plan), `up` lists it in `plan.invocations`, and when the apply reaches it the call
returns `awaiting_actions` with the request's `prompt` and `inputs`. You do the step with
your own tools and answer every open request in one call:

```
apply({ convergence_id, action_results: {
  "<key>": { succeeded: true,  progress: ["what you did, a line each"] },
  "<key>": { succeeded: false, progress: ["asked the user"],
             diagnostics: [{ severity: "error", summary: "why it failed" }] } } })
```

Three patterns, and the journeys use all of them:

| Pattern | What the prompt asks | Bound how |
|---|---|---|
| **Verify** | check something with your tools; pass or fail | `after_create` with `on_failure = taint` (on any other event a failure halts), or `before_create` with `halt` as a pre-flight |
| **Ask** | a decision only the user can make | `before_*` with `halt` — or declared with no trigger, for `invoke({ action_addr })` on demand |
| **Announce** | a notification | `after_*` with `on_failure = continue`; a failed notice only warns |

A turf action is an apply-time step, not a second approval: by the time it runs the plan is
approved. That is the point when the configuration's author wants a step a run cannot skip —
an apply the agent approved itself still stops for it. Answering one in full:
[`read_skill_file({ skill_name: "deployment", path: "references/turf-actions.md" })`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/turf-actions/); declaring
one: [`skill_authoring → references/actions.md`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/actions/).

## The examples

The journeys run from a checkout of
[turfbuild/turf-examples](https://github.com/turfbuild/turf-examples). Find it in this
order, and say which you used: `TURF_EXAMPLES_DIR`; a `turf-examples` directory in or
beside the working directory; otherwise offer
`git clone https://github.com/turfbuild/turf-examples` into the working directory. Each
journey names its example's path under that checkout.

The engine runs provider plugins, and the actions that shell out (`kubectl`, `git`), with
the Turf service's environment — not your shell's. If a step needs a tool on the engine's
`PATH`, the journey says so.

## The menu

Offer these as questions, in this order, and recommend **Deploy AICR → Day 2** as the path
for anyone new: one cluster, deployed then operated, is the whole story in two journeys.
Each journey loads from a reference file — fetch it with
`read_skill_file({ skill_name: "guide", path: "references/<name>.md" })` and run its beats.
Every journey needs [`skill_deployment`](/docs/reference/skills/deployment/); one marked _edits configuration_ also needs
[`skill_authoring`](/docs/reference/skills/authoring/) before its first `.tf` or `*.turf.hcl` write.

| Would you like to… | `path` | Example | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **deploy the NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) on a cluster — from nothing, in one command?** _(start here)_ | [`references/deploy-aicr.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/deploy-aicr/) | `use-cases/datacenter/aicr-stack` | Docker, kind, kubectl; no GPU, no cloud credentials |
| **run day 2 — take a node through the maintenance runbook, every step a Terraform action?** | [`references/day2-maintenance.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/day2-maintenance/) | `terraform/kubernetes/node-maintenance` | the AICR cluster from the first journey (or any cluster with two workers); kubectl on the engine's PATH |
| **make your product an autonomous infrastructure layer — a smart installer?** | [`references/installer.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/installer/) | `use-cases/products/data-lake-installer` | nothing (plan-only, no cloud account) |
| **promote a change across environments — one configuration, a stack per environment?** | [`references/promotion.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/promotion/) | `terraform/language/environments` _(edits configuration)_ | nothing (credential-free) |
| **work with your TACO — state, variables and policy in Scalr or HCP Terraform, Turf as the engine?** | [`references/taco.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/taco/) | `integrations/scalr` _(edits configuration)_ | a TACO account and a CLI token (`turf login <host>`); narrated without one |
| **deploy with guardrails — scan every provider before it runs, pin the workload, and check every plan against policy?** | [`references/guardrails.md`](/docs/reference/skills/guide/guardrails/) | `use-cases/guardrails` | trivy or grype, and opa or conftest, on the PATH (or their MCP servers); Docker + kind |

## Opening move

- If the user named a topic (the `/guide` prompt may pass one), treat it as free-form intent:
  map it to the closest journey above, load its reference file, and begin its first beat
  (jump to a specific beat if the topic names one). If two fit, offer just those; if none
  does, present the menu.
- Otherwise: three sentences on what Turf is and that this is hands-on; the menu above as
  questions; the recommendation (Deploy AICR, then Day 2); and ask which they'd like. Then
  load the chosen reference and start. End on a cue.
